title: 30-Day Content Calendar
summary: Set up a posting rhythm you can keep for 30 days on under three hours a week, and learn which format your audience actually wants.
output: A filled-in 30-day calendar, three content pillars, one batching slot on your calendar and a tracker that shows which format hit.

sections.heading: Pick your three pillars before you film anything
sections.body:
Most people quit posting because every day starts with a blank screen. Pillars fix that. A pillar is a topic bucket you can pull from forever. Three is enough. More than three and your page looks random. Fewer and you run dry.

Eli's approach to audience growth comes down to four things: be authentic, be consistent, find the format that hits and reuse it, and lead with your personal brand. People follow people before they follow businesses. So at least one pillar should be about you: what you're learning, what you're building, what went wrong.

A good pillar set has one that teaches, one that shows proof, and one that shows you.
steps: Teach: the problem your customer has and how to fix part of it for free.
Proof: work you did, before and afters, customer words, what you're testing.
You: your story, your week, your mistakes, why you started.
sections.example: A sneaker cleaning side business: (1) Teach: how to get creases and stains out at home. (2) Proof: before and after clips of real pairs. (3) You: a 20-year-old building a business between classes, the wins and the pairs that went wrong.

sections.heading: Choose one main platform
sections.body:
You have under three hours a week. You do not have time to win on five platforms. Pick the one where your customer already scrolls, post there first, and repurpose the same clip elsewhere only if it costs you under five minutes.

Quick guide: TikTok and Instagram Reels for consumer products and local services. YouTube Shorts if you also want longer videos later. LinkedIn if you sell to businesses or professionals (a resume-review offer fits here). X if your customers are founders, developers or creators who read more than they watch.

sections.heading: The weekly rhythm
sections.body: Consistency beats volume. Three to five posts a week that you actually publish will do more than a daily plan you abandon in week two. Here is a five-day rhythm built on the three pillars. Drop to three days (Monday, Wednesday, Friday) if that's what you can keep.
bullets: Monday (Teach): one quick how-to or one mistake to avoid.
Tuesday (You): a lesson you learned this week, told as a short story.
Wednesday (Proof): a before and after, a result, or a customer's exact words (real only, with permission).
Thursday (Teach): answer a question someone actually asked you.
Friday (You): behind the scenes. Show the work, the setup, the messy part.

sections.heading: Batch a week in two hours with CapCut
sections.body: Posting every day does not mean filming every day. Block one two-hour slot a week and make everything at once. Eli used CapCut on his iPhone for fast edits. It's free and good enough to start.
steps: 15 minutes: write five hooks and five one-line outlines, one per post. Use your pillars and last week's comments for ideas.
45 minutes: film all five back to back. Same spot, same light, change your shirt if you care. Shoot each hook two or three ways.
45 minutes: edit in CapCut. Cut every pause, add auto captions, keep most videos under 45 seconds.
15 minutes: write captions and schedule them (native scheduler, or a Notion board if you want to track ideas and status in one place).
sections.example: A tutoring service for high school math: Sunday 4 to 6 pm. Five videos: a common algebra mistake, why the tutor almost failed calculus, a student's grade jump (with permission), a viewer's question answered, and a look at how a session is planned.

sections.heading: Your 30-day calendar
sections.body: Copy this into Notes, Notion or a Google Doc and fill in the blanks during your first batching session. Each row is one post. Fill week one completely now. Fill weeks two to four with topics only, then sharpen them as you learn what hits.

sections.heading: Track which format hits
sections.body:
A format is the shape of the video, not the topic. Talking head with a text hook. Green screen over a screenshot. Voiceover on a before and after. A list of three. A day-in-the-life. Change one thing at a time so you know what made the difference.

When a post beats your average, Eli's question is: why? What did this one do that the others didn't? Then reuse that format or framework until it stops working. Do more of what works, not just more.
sections.template:
FORMAT TRACKER (fill in 48 hours after posting)
Date | Pillar | Format | Hook | Views | Saves/Shares | Comments | Profile visits or DMs
[ ] | [ ] | [ ] | [ ] | [ ] | [ ] | [ ] | [ ]

End of each week:
My average views: [ ]
Post that beat it: [ ]
Why I think it worked: [ ]
Next week I'll reuse: [format or hook]
bullets: Views tell you if the hook stopped the scroll.
Saves and shares tell you the content was useful.
Comments and DMs tell you it built trust. These are the ones that turn into customers.
Give a format at least three tries before you judge it. One post is noise.

sections.heading: What you leave with
sections.body: By the end of this session you should have three pillars written down, one platform chosen, a two-hour batching slot blocked on your calendar, week one fully planned and the first format you're going to test. Then make today day one: batch your first five posts this week. Fill in the worksheet below so you can come back and check yourself at day 30.

worksheet.label: Pillar 1: what will you teach?
worksheet.placeholder: e.g. how to clean sneakers at home

worksheet.label: Pillar 2: what proof will you show?
Pillar 3: what part of you and your story will you share?
Your main platform
Which days will you post?
Your weekly two-hour batching slot
The format you'll test first, and why
worksheet.placeholder: e.g. voiceover on a before and after, because results are my strongest proof

aiPrompt: Check that the three pillars are distinct and tied to a real customer problem, that one pillar features the member personally, that the posting days and batching slot are realistic for someone with under three hours a week, and that the first format is specific enough to test.

title: Hook & Caption Bank
summary: Fill-in-the-blank hooks, captions and calls to action so you never start a post from a blank screen.
output: Ten hooks written for your niche, three captions ready to post, your go-to CTA, and a loop for doubling down on the format that works.

sections.heading: How to use this bank
sections.body:
The first line decides whether anyone sees the rest. A hook is a promise: keep watching and you'll get this. Don't copy these word for word. Fill the blanks with your customer's exact words, then say it out loud. If it sounds like an ad, rewrite it until it sounds like you.

Rules for every hook:
bullets: Say it in the first two seconds, on screen and out loud.
One idea per post. If the hook promises two things, split it into two posts.
Be specific. Numbers, names of tools, places and timeframes beat vague words.
Only claim what's true. A fake result might get views, but it costs you trust, and trust beats everything.
Write five hooks for every post and pick the best one. Test the runner-up next time.

sections.heading: Story and mistake hooks
sections.body: Story hooks work because people follow people. Mistake hooks work because nobody wants to make the same one.
sections.template:
STORY
1. I started [business] with [small amount or resource]. Here's what happened.
2. A year ago I was [old situation]. Today I'm [new situation].
3. The day I almost quit [thing] was the day [turning point].
4. My first customer for [offer] came from [unexpected place].
5. Nobody believed [thing] would work. Here's what I did anyway.
6. This is what [number] weeks of building [business] looks like.
7. I didn't think I was qualified to [goal]. Here's what changed.

MISTAKE
8. I wasted [time or money] on [thing] so you don't have to.
9. The biggest mistake I made starting [business]: [mistake].
10. Stop [common action] if you want [result].
11. [Number] mistakes I made in my first [timeframe] of [business].
12. If you're doing [common habit], you're losing [result].
13. I tried [popular advice]. It didn't work. Here's why.
14. Don't [action] until you've done this first.

sections.heading: Contrarian and how-to hooks
sections.body: Contrarian hooks earn attention by disagreeing with something your audience has heard a hundred times. Only use one if you actually believe it and can back it up. How-to hooks are your most reliable saves.
sections.template:
CONTRARIAN
15. Unpopular opinion: you don't need [common belief] to [result].
16. Everyone says [advice]. I think that's wrong.
17. [Popular thing] is overrated. Do this instead.
18. The worst advice I got about [topic]: [advice].
19. You don't have a [problem] problem. You have a [real problem] problem.
20. Nobody talks about this part of [topic].
21. [Thing people fear] isn't the hard part. [Real hard part] is.

HOW-TO
22. How to [result] in [timeframe] without [pain].
23. Here's exactly how I'd [result] if I started today.
24. [Number] steps to [result]. Save this.
25. The [number]-minute fix for [problem].
26. How I [result] using only [tool or phone].
27. Do this before you [common action].
28. The easiest way to [result] for [specific person].

sections.heading: Result and behind-the-scenes hooks
sections.body: Result hooks only work with real results. If you don't have one yet, use a customer's result (with permission) or a small honest win. Behind-the-scenes hooks build trust because they show the work, not just the outcome.
sections.template:
RESULT
29. This [before] became [after] in [timeframe].
30. How [customer type] went from [before] to [after].
31. What [price or amount] gets you with [offer].
32. We just [milestone]. Here's what actually made the difference.
33. Watch this [thing] go from [before] to [after].
34. [Customer] said [exact quote]. Here's what we did.
35. My [first / tenth / best] [sale, client, drop] and what I learned.

BEHIND THE SCENES
36. A day running [business] while [other commitment].
37. What goes into one [product or service] that nobody sees.
38. Packing orders for [business]. Come with me.
39. Here's what my [setup / workspace / process] actually looks like.
40. The part of [business] I hate, and why I do it anyway.
41. Honest update: week [number] of building [business].
42. Here's how a [service] session actually goes.
sections.example: A short-form video editing service, filled in: 'This 40-minute podcast became 6 clips in one afternoon.' (Result, #29.) 'Here's exactly how I'd get my first editing client if I started today.' (How-to, #23.) 'You don't have a views problem. You have a first-two-seconds problem.' (Contrarian, #19.)

sections.heading: 10 caption templates
sections.body: The hook gets the view. The caption keeps the reader and gives them a next step. Keep it short on TikTok and Reels, longer on LinkedIn and X.
sections.template:
1. QUICK LESSON
[Hook restated]. Here's what I learned: [lesson in one sentence]. [CTA]

2. THREE TIPS
[Number] things I wish I knew about [topic]:
1) [tip]
2) [tip]
3) [tip]
Which one are you trying first?

3. BEFORE / AFTER
Before: [situation]. After: [situation]. What changed: [one thing]. [CTA]

4. MISTAKE
I used to [mistake]. It cost me [cost]. Now I [new habit]. Don't repeat my mistake.

5. CUSTOMER WORDS
'[exact customer quote].' That's why we [what you do]. [CTA]

6. STORY
[Where you were]. [What happened]. [What you learned]. [Question for the reader]

7. BEHIND THE SCENES
What you didn't see: [hidden work]. This is why [result] takes [time].

8. QUESTION
Honest question for [audience]: [question]? I'll reply to every comment.

9. OFFER
I help [who] [get result] without [pain]. I'm taking [number] [clients / orders] this month. [CTA]

10. MYTH
Myth: [common belief]. Truth: [what you've seen]. Here's why: [reason].

sections.heading: 10 calls to action
sections.body: Every post gets one CTA, never three. Match it to your goal: comments help reach, saves signal value, DMs start conversations, and links drive sales. ManyChat can send an automatic DM when someone comments a keyword, which makes the 'comment a word' CTA easy to run on Instagram.
bullets: Comment '[keyword]' and I'll send you [free thing].
Save this for the next time you [situation].
Send this to someone who needs to [result].
Follow for part two.
DM me '[keyword]' if you want help with [problem].
Which one are you? Tell me in the comments.
Link in bio to [book / order / get the free guide].
Follow if you're building [type of business] too.
Try this today and tell me how it goes.
I'm taking [number] [clients / orders] this week. DM me to grab a spot.

sections.heading: The do-more-of-what-works loop
sections.body: A hook bank only matters if you learn from it. Eli grew his social channels by doubling down: when a video worked, he reused that format or framework to hit again. Run this loop every week.
steps: Post. Use hooks from at least two different types this week so you have a comparison.
Wait 48 hours. Note views, saves, shares and DMs for each post.
Find the winner. Which post beat your average clearly?
Ask why. Was it the hook type, the topic, the format, the length, the first frame? Write down one reason.
Double down. Make three new posts that keep the winning element and change everything else.
Repeat until it stops working. When a format drops below your average twice in a row, pause it and test a new hook type.
sections.template:
WINNING POST REVIEW
Post: [link]
Hook type: [story / mistake / contrarian / how-to / result / BTS]
What it did differently: [ ]
Why I think it worked: [ ]
Three remixes:
1. [same element, new topic]
2. [same element, new topic]
3. [same element, new topic]

sections.heading: Your output
sections.body: Before you close this, write ten hooks for your niche (at least one from each type), fill in three caption templates, and pick the one CTA you'll use most this month. Save them in your notes app or your content board so your next batching session starts with a full list.

worksheet.label: Who are you talking to, in one line?
worksheet.placeholder: e.g. college students who want clean sneakers without paying retail

worksheet.label: Write ten hooks for your niche (one per line, at least one from each type)
worksheet.placeholder: 1. I wasted $200 on cleaning kits so you don't have to...

worksheet.label: Fill in three caption templates
Your go-to CTA this month
worksheet.placeholder: e.g. Comment CLEAN and I'll send you my stain guide

worksheet.label: Your best post so far: what made it work?
worksheet.placeholder: Hook type, format, why you think it beat the others

aiPrompt: Check that the hooks are specific to the member's niche with real words, numbers or tools rather than generic blanks, that every hook type is represented, that no hook claims a fake result, and that the CTA matches a clear goal.

title: Outreach Scripts
summary: Copyable messages for warm outreach, cold DMs, follow-ups, inbound replies, booking calls and asking for referrals, without sounding like a bot.
output: A list of 20 warm contacts, your first message written and sent, and a simple tracker for follow-ups.

sections.heading: Start with 20 people who already know you
sections.body:
Your first customers almost never come from strangers. They come from people who already trust you, or from people those people trust. Eli's rule: trust beats everything else in sales. Win their trust, win their wallet.

Before you write a single message, open your contacts, your DMs and your follower list and write down 20 names. Not 20 buyers. 20 people who might buy, know someone who would, or give you honest feedback.
bullets: Friends and family who'd tell you the truth.
Classmates, teammates, coworkers, old bosses.
People in group chats or clubs you're part of.
Followers who've commented or replied to you before.
Anyone who's ever asked you for help with the thing you now sell.

sections.heading: Warm outreach: people you know
sections.body: Be direct. People you know can tell when you're being weird. Say what you started, who it's for, and ask for one small thing: feedback, a referral, or a yes. Personalize the first line every time.
sections.template:
WARM: ASK FOR FEEDBACK
Hey [name], [one real personal line, e.g. saw you started at the new job, congrats]. I just started [business], helping [who] with [problem]. Before I go wider, I'd love your honest take. Can I send you a 30-second overview?

WARM: DIRECT OFFER
Hey [name], quick one. I'm doing [service] for [who] and taking my first [number] clients at [intro price or bonus]. You mentioned [problem they told you about] a while back. Is that still a thing for you?

WARM: ASK WHO THEY KNOW
Hey [name], I started [business]. I help [who] [get result]. Do you know anyone dealing with [problem] right now? Even one name helps a ton.
sections.example: A lawn care service: 'Hey Marcus, hope the new semester's going well. I started a lawn care service this spring, mostly mowing and edging for families in [neighborhood]. Your parents mentioned last summer the yard was a lot to keep up with. Would they want a free first cut so they can see the work?'

sections.heading: Cold DMs that don't feel spammy
sections.body: Cold works when it's clearly written for one person. Eli's life hack is to talk to everyone, everywhere, every time, but that means real conversations, not copy-paste blasts. Three rules: mention something specific about them, ask about their situation before you offer anything, and keep it under four lines.
sections.template:
COLD: START WITH THEM
Hey [name], saw your [post / video / store] about [specific thing]. [Genuine one-line reaction]. Curious, how are you handling [problem] right now?

COLD: USEFUL FIRST
Hey [name], I [do thing] for [type of person]. I noticed [specific, small issue, e.g. your last three reels have no captions]. Happy to send a quick tip on fixing it, no strings. Want it?

COLD: AFTER THEY REPLY WITH THE PROBLEM
That makes sense. A lot of [type of person] I talk to say the same. I actually help with exactly that: [one-line offer]. Want me to show you how it'd work for you?
bullets: Never open with a pitch or a link.
Never send the same message to 50 people at once.
If they don't describe a problem, don't offer. Thank them and move on.
Ask how they solve it today. Their answer tells you whether your offer fits.

sections.heading: Follow-ups
sections.body: Most replies come after a follow-up, because people are busy, not because they said no. Follow up once after three days, once more after a week, then stop. Each follow-up should add something, not just bump the thread.
sections.template:
FOLLOW-UP 1 (day 3)
Hey [name], just floating this back up in case it got buried. No pressure either way.

FOLLOW-UP 2 (day 7, add value)
Hey [name], thought of you when I [made this / saw this]: [link or tip]. Still happy to chat about [problem] whenever works.

CLOSE THE LOOP (day 14)
Hey [name], I'll stop bugging you. If [problem] ever becomes a priority, I'm here. Appreciate you.

sections.heading: Replying to inbound and booking the call
sections.body: When someone reaches out first, speed matters. Reply the same day. Ask one or two questions to understand their situation before quoting a price. Then move to a short call or a clear next step. A Calendly link makes booking easy.
sections.template:
INBOUND: FIRST REPLY
Hey [name], thanks for reaching out. Quick question so I can actually help: what's going on with [problem] right now, and what have you tried so far?

INBOUND: AFTER THEY EXPLAIN
Got it. That's exactly what I help with. The fastest way to see if it's a fit is a 15-minute call. Grab any time here: [booking link]. Or tell me two times that work.

BOOKING: CONFIRM
You're booked for [day, time]. I'll come with [one thing you'll prepare, e.g. three ideas for your page]. If anything changes, just reply here.

SIMPLE OFFER AFTER THE CALL
Great talking, [name]. Here's what we discussed: [their problem in their words]. What I'll do: [deliverable] by [date]. Price: [price]. If you're in, reply YES and I'll send [payment link / next step].
sections.example: A resume-review offer on LinkedIn: 'Got it, you've applied to 40 roles and heard back from two. That's exactly what I help with. I'll rewrite your resume for one target role and send it back in 48 hours. Price: [price]. If you don't land at least one interview from your next 15 applications, I'll do a second round free.' Frame cost as the smallest number and value as the largest.

sections.heading: Asking for referrals
sections.body: The best time to ask is right after a customer says something good. Make it easy: tell them exactly who to send and give them a message they can forward.
sections.template:
REFERRAL ASK
Really glad [result] worked out, [name]. Quick ask: do you know one or two people who are dealing with [problem]? If it helps, here's a message you can forward:

'Hey, I used [your name] for [service] and [result]. Thought of you. Here's their [link / handle].'

REFERRAL THANK YOU
Hey [name], [referred person] reached out because of you. Thank you. [Small thank-you, e.g. your next [service] is on me].

sections.heading: Integrity rules
sections.body: How you do one thing is how people think you do everything. Your DMs are your reputation. Eli's standard is simple: no shady deals, no unkept promises, no manipulation.
bullets: No fake scarcity. Only say 'three spots left' if there are three spots left.
No fake urgency, fake results or fake testimonials.
No guilt trips. A no is a no. Thank them and leave the door open.
Don't promise what you can't deliver. Under-promise, over-deliver.
Respect platform rules and people's inboxes. If someone asks you to stop, stop.
If your offer won't help them, say so and point them somewhere that will.

sections.heading: Track it and send your first message today
sections.body: Outreach dies without tracking. You'll forget who you messaged and when to follow up. A notes app works. A spreadsheet works. Attio works if you want a real CRM as you grow. Pick one tonight.
sections.template:
OUTREACH TRACKER
Name | How I know them | Date sent | Script used | Replied? | Follow-up date | Outcome
[ ] | [ ] | [ ] | [ ] | [Y/N] | [ ] | [call / sale / referral / no]

worksheet.label: List 20 warm contacts (name and how you know them, one per line)
worksheet.placeholder:
1. Marcus, high school teammate
2. Aunt Jo, owns a salon...

worksheet.label: The exact message you'll send first
What day will you send follow-ups?
worksheet.placeholder: e.g. Thursday, three days after sending

worksheet.label: How will you track replies and follow-ups?

aiPrompt: Check that the contact list has close to 20 real names with context, that the first message is personalized, short and asks about the person's problem before pitching, that it avoids fake scarcity or pressure, and that there is a concrete follow-up day and tracking method.

title: Founder KPI Dashboard
summary: Track the five numbers that show where your business leaks, and decide each week what to kill, pause or double down on.
output: A weekly scorecard with your five numbers, the conversion rate between each step, and one decision for next week.

sections.heading: Fill in last week's numbers first
sections.body:
Don't read the rest until you've entered last week in the scorecard above. Guesses are fine for week one. Write down where each number came from so next week is faster: your platform analytics, your site dashboard, your DMs, your payment app.

If a number is zero, enter zero. A zero is information. It tells you exactly where to look.

sections.heading: The five numbers
sections.body: Every early business runs on the same chain: people see you, some get curious, some start a conversation, some buy, and that turns into money. Track these five every week, same day, same sources.
steps: Reach: total views or impressions across your content, ads or flyers. How many people saw you.
Visits: profile visits or website visitors. How many got curious enough to look closer.
Leads: DMs, form fills, booked calls or real conversations. How many raised their hand.
Sales: number of paying customers or orders. How many said yes with money.
Revenue: total money in from those sales. Not profit, just what came in. Your bookkeeping (and a professional, when you need one) handles the rest.

sections.heading: What each conversion rate tells you
sections.body: The dashboard divides each step by the one before it. That rate is where the real lesson is. A big number with a bad rate after it is a leak. Fix the leak before you pour more people in the top. More reach on a leaky page just means more people leaving.
bullets: Reach to visits (visits divided by reach): is your content making people curious about you? If it's low, your hooks get views but your profile or offer isn't clear. Fix your bio, pinned posts and first line of your site.
Visits to leads (leads divided by visits): when people look closer, do they reach out? If it's low, your offer or your CTA is weak. Make the next step obvious and the offer clearer.
Leads to sales (sales divided by leads): when people talk to you, do they buy? If it's low, it's your conversation, your price framing or your offer. Reread your DMs. Use the outreach scripts.
Revenue per sale (revenue divided by sales): what's each customer worth? If it's low, look at pricing, bundles or an upsell. Tie the price to the ROI the customer sees.
sections.example: A print-on-demand brand's week: 12,000 views, 300 profile visits, 20 DMs, 4 orders, $140 revenue. Reach to visits is 2.5%, visits to leads about 6.7%, leads to sales 20%, $35 per sale. The content is working fine. The leak is between visits and DMs: people look at the page and leave. Next week's fix is the bio and a pinned post that shows the best designs and how to order.

sections.heading: Read week-over-week, not day to day
sections.body:
One good day means nothing. One week is a data point. Three weeks is a trend. The dashboard shows the change from last week for every number. Look for the step that moved most, up or down, and ask what you did differently.

When something works, Eli's question is: why? What did this do that everything before didn't? Then do more of that until it stops working. Do more of what works, not just more.
bullets: Reach up, everything else flat: you found a hook, but it's attracting the wrong people or your next step is unclear.
Reach flat, sales up: your conversations or offer improved. Figure out what you said differently and write it down.
Everything down: you probably posted less or messaged fewer people. Check your inputs before you change the strategy.

sections.heading: Kill, pause or double down
sections.body: Every week, look at what you spent time on and match it to the numbers. Then make one call per activity. Product-market fit, in Eli's words, is when people want to pay without you needing to sell them. Until then, your numbers are how you find the path to it.
bullets: Double down: the activity moved a number you care about for two or more weeks. Do more of exactly that. Same format, same channel, same message.
Pause: it hasn't moved anything yet, but you've run it fewer than three times or changed too many things at once. Run it cleanly one more time, then decide.
Kill: you've given it a fair try and it hasn't moved leads or sales. Stop. Time is the only thing you can't buy back, and you have under three hours a week.
sections.template:
WEEKLY DECISION
The step with the biggest leak: [reach / visits / leads / sales / revenue per sale]
What I think is causing it: [ ]
Double down on: [activity]
Pause: [activity]
Kill: [activity]
One change I'll test next week: [ ]

sections.heading: Make it a Monday habit
sections.body: Ten minutes, same time every week. Enter the numbers, read the rates, make the call, then plan your week around the biggest leak. Pair it with the Weekly CEO Review so the numbers turn into next week's top three. Keep every week's scorecard. After a month you'll be able to see which changes actually moved the numbers, and which ones only felt productive.
steps: Pull last week's numbers from the same sources every time.
Enter them in the scorecard.
Find the lowest conversion rate and the biggest week-over-week change.
Write one kill, one pause and one double down.
Put the one test for next week on your calendar.

sections.heading: What you walk away with
sections.body: A filled-in scorecard for last week, the conversion rate at every step, the one leak you're fixing next, and a written kill, pause or double down call. Do it again next Monday and you'll have your first week-over-week trend.

title: Weekly CEO Review
summary: A 30-minute weekly review that pulls you out of the busywork and decides what next week is for.
output: A completed review with your numbers, what to double down on, what to cut, one thing to delegate or automate, next week's top three and a perspective check.

sections.heading: Book the 30 minutes now
sections.body:
Put a recurring 30-minute block on your calendar before you read any further. Sunday evening or Monday morning works for most people. Same time, every week, phone on do not disturb.

Eli's principle: get to the point where you're working on the business, not in it, as fast as you can. Your business is only as valuable as it is when you aren't there to run it. You won't get there by accident. This review is the 30 minutes a week where you act like the CEO instead of the only employee.

sections.heading: The six parts
sections.body: Each part has a time box. Stick to it. The point is a decision, not a journal entry.
steps: Numbers (5 minutes): enter last week's reach, visits, leads, sales and revenue in the KPI Dashboard. Note the biggest change.
What worked and why (5 minutes): name the one thing that moved a number. Ask why it worked better than what came before.
What to cut (5 minutes): name what took time and produced nothing. Kill it or pause it.
Delegate or automate (5 minutes): name one task you did that someone or something else could do.
Next week's top three (5 minutes): pick the three things that will move the numbers most. Three, not ten.
Perspective check (5 minutes): step back from the business and check what matters more than it.

sections.heading: Numbers, wins and cuts
sections.body:
Start with numbers because feelings lie. A week that felt busy can be a week where nothing moved. A week that felt slow can be the week you got your first referral.

For wins, don't stop at 'that post did well'. Ask what it did that the others didn't. Was it the hook, the offer, who you messaged, the time you posted? Do more of what works, not just more.

For cuts, be honest. Trying to do too much was one of Eli's biggest mistakes. There are a million ways to make money. Pick one, get really good at it. Every week, something should come off your list.
sections.example: A short-form video editing service: Numbers show 6 leads, 2 sales. What worked: a before-and-after clip of a client's podcast got 4 of the 6 DMs, because it showed the result in the first second. What to cut: two hours spent redesigning the logo, zero impact. Decision: make three more before-and-after clips next week, logo stays as is.

sections.heading: Delegate or automate one thing
sections.body: You don't need a team to start delegating. Look at your week and find the tasks you repeat that don't need your judgment. Some can go to AI or an automation. Some can go to a freelancer later. Write it down now even if you can't hand it off yet. The list becomes your plan.
bullets: Repeated DM replies: a saved reply, or ManyChat for keyword-triggered messages.
Call notes and follow-ups: Granola to capture notes, then a follow-up template.
Content ideas, captions and first drafts: Claude, with your hook bank as input.
Research on competitors or a market: Perplexity.
Scheduling: a Calendly link instead of back-and-forth texts.
Bigger repeat tasks: write a one-page process and see the Delegate Your First Task playbook.

sections.heading: Next week's top three
sections.body:
Each one should be specific, finishable in a week and tied to a number. 'Grow on TikTok' is not a top three item. 'Post four before-and-after clips and reply to every comment within a day' is.

If everything feels important, ask: if I only got one of these done, which would move revenue or customers the most? That's number one.

Then put all three on your calendar before you close the review. A priority without a time slot is a wish. If you can't find the time for all three, that's your answer: cut one, or delegate something from step four.

sections.heading: Perspective check
sections.body: 127 is built on Psalm 127:1: unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain. Building in vain, as Eli puts it, means only focusing on money while neglecting your faith and the people who matter. Take two minutes on each question. Purpose over profit.
bullets: Did I keep my commitments to the people closest to me this week?
Did I make time for my faith, rest and health, or did the business eat all of it?
Did I do business with integrity: no shortcuts, no promises I couldn't keep?
Who helped me this week, and have I thanked them? Nobody is self-made.
Am I still building for the reason I started?

sections.heading: The template
sections.body: Copy this into Notion, Google Docs or your notes app. Duplicate it every week so you can look back and see the trend.

aiPrompt: Check that the numbers are filled in, that 'what worked' includes a real reason rather than a description, that something was actually cut, that the top three are specific, finishable in a week and tied to a number, and that the perspective check was answered honestly rather than skipped.

title: Delegate Your First Task
summary: Find the task that eats your week, write it down so someone or something else can run it, and hand it off for good.
output: A last-week hours audit, a one-page SOP for your first task, and that task handed to a person, AI tool or automation.

sections.heading: Audit last week's hours
sections.body:
You can't hand off what you can't see. Open your calendar, your screen time, your texts and your notes from last week and list every task you did for the business, with rough time spent. Be honest. Twenty minutes answering the same DM five times counts.

Then tag each one.
bullets: Only me: needs your judgment, your face or your relationships. Selling, key decisions, being on camera.
Repeat: you do it the same way every time. Replying to common questions, posting, invoicing, scheduling.
Waste: it didn't need doing at all. Cut it today.
sections.template:
HOURS AUDIT (last week)
Task | Time spent | How often | Tag (only me / repeat / waste)
[ ] | [ ] | [daily / weekly] | [ ]
[ ] | [ ] | [ ] | [ ]
[ ] | [ ] | [ ] | [ ]

Total hours: [ ]
Hours on 'repeat' tasks: [ ]
Hours on 'waste': [ ]

sections.heading: Why this matters now
sections.body:
Two of Eli's principles drive this playbook. First: get to the point where you're working on the business, not in it, as fast as you can. Second: your business is only as valuable as it is when you aren't there to run it. If every task lives in your head, you don't have a business yet. You have a job you made for yourself.

You don't need money or a team to start. Your first handoff might be to an AI tool or a free automation. The skill is writing the process down. That skill is what lets you hire later.

sections.heading: Pick your first task
sections.body: Don't start with the hardest thing. Start with the task that is repeated, rule-based and low-risk if it goes wrong once. Score your 'repeat' tasks and pick the winner.
steps: How often does it happen? Weekly or more is ideal.
Can you explain the steps without saying 'it depends' more than once?
If it's done slightly worse than you'd do it, does anything break? If not, it's a good first task.
How much time would it free up each week?
sections.example: A sneaker cleaning side business: the owner spends about two hours a week answering 'how much for a deep clean?' and 'how long does it take?' in DMs. It happens every day, the answers never change, and a slightly slow reply doesn't lose a customer. That's the first task. Second place: photographing before and afters, which needs more judgment, so it waits.

sections.heading: Write a one-page SOP
sections.body: SOP means standard operating procedure: a written set of steps anyone could follow. The fastest way to write one is to record yourself doing the task once with your phone's screen recorder, talking out loud. Then write the steps from the recording. Claude can turn a transcript or rough notes into a clean draft for you to edit. Keep it to one page. If it's longer, the task is too big. Split it.
sections.template:
SOP: [task name]
Owner: [who or what runs this]
How often: [daily / weekly / when X happens]
Time it should take: [ ]

WHY THIS MATTERS
[One sentence: what this task does for the customer or the business]

WHAT YOU NEED
- Access to: [tools, accounts, folders]
- Templates or saved replies: [link]

STEPS
1. [ ]
2. [ ]
3. [ ]
4. [ ]
5. [ ]

WHAT GOOD LOOKS LIKE
[Example of a finished result, or a link to one]

COMMON MISTAKES
- [ ]
- [ ]

WHEN TO ASK ME
[The exact situations that need the owner, e.g. refunds, angry customers, anything over $X]

Recording: [link to screen recording]

sections.heading: Choose who or what runs it
sections.body: Match the task to the cheapest option that will do it well. Don't hire a person for something a saved reply can handle.
bullets: Saved replies or templates: free, best for answers that never change.
Automation: ManyChat for DM keyword replies on Instagram, Calendly for booking, Shopify for order confirmations, Klaviyo for email follow-ups. Best for 'when X happens, do Y' tasks.
AI tools: Claude for drafting captions, emails or first versions of content, Granola for call notes, Perplexity for research. You still review the output.
A freelancer: for tasks that need a human, like video editing, design or customer support. Start with one small, paid test task. Check local rules or a professional before treating anyone as staff.
A friend or family member: only with clear expectations and fair pay. Choosing the right people to build with is crucial. A bad fit costs more than money.
sections.example: A tutoring service: scheduling and reminders go to Calendly with automatic text reminders. Writing weekly progress notes for parents goes to Claude, using the tutor's session notes and a template, with the tutor reviewing each one before sending.

sections.heading: Review the first three runs
sections.body: Handoffs fail when you either hover over every step or disappear completely. Do neither. Review the first three runs closely, then step back.
steps: Run 1: watch or check everything. Note each place they got stuck or the result was off.
Fix the SOP, not just the result. If the same question comes up twice, the answer goes in the document.
Run 2: check the finished result only. Give one or two pieces of specific feedback.
Run 3: spot check. If it's 80 percent as good as you'd do it, that's a pass.
After run 3, switch to a quick weekly check during your Weekly CEO Review.

sections.heading: Let go
sections.body:
The last step is the hardest. It won't be done exactly your way. That's fine. If it's done well and consistently, your time is now free for the work only you can do: selling, building relationships, improving the product. Treat whoever helps you the way you'd want to be treated: clear instructions, fair pay, credit when it goes well.

Your output from this playbook: a completed hours audit, one task chosen on purpose, a one-page SOP saved where you can share it, and a named person or tool running it. Then go back to your audit and pick the next one.
